Task: Develop a complete lesson plan for teaching probability to high-school students.

High-School Probability Lesson Plan (1–2 class periods, 50 min each)

————————————————————————
1. Lesson Overview
————————————————————————
Topic    Introduction to basic probability  
Grade    9–10 (adaptable 8–12)  
Duration  1 × 50-min period (core) + 1 × 50-min extension/lab  
Prerequisites Fractions, ratios, basic set notation, reading bar charts/tables  
Objectives By the end of the lesson, students will be able to  
 • Define and use the terms experiment, outcome, sample space, event, probability  
 • Compute theoretical probability of simple events (single stage and independent two-stage)  
 • Distinguish experimental (empirical) from theoretical probability  
 • Simulate probability with manipulatives or digital tools and compare to theory  
 • Recognize when outcomes are equally likely and explain assumptions

————————————————————————
2. Standards Alignment (examples, US Common Core)
————————————————————————
CCSS.MATH.CONTENT.HSS.IC.A.1 Understand statistics as a process for making inferences; distinguish between theoretical and experimental probability  
CCSS.MATH.CONTENT.HSS.CP.A.1-5 Understand and apply basic probability rules, including compound events and independence

————————————————————————
3. Materials & Resources
————————————————————————
• 30 fair coins  
• 30 six-sided dice  
• Decks of standard playing cards (optional)  
• Small colored counters (red/blue/green/yellow, 20 each group)  
• Document camera or interactive board  
• Handouts: guided notes, exit ticket, homework sheet  
• Digital: Free virtual dice/coin simulator (e.g., on Desmos / GeoGebra) for extension  
• Probability anchor chart (vocabulary) posted on wall

————————————————————————
4. Lesson Flow
————————————————————————
Period 1 (50 min)

0–5 min HOOK  
 Teacher tosses a coin three times, records H-T pattern. Ask: “What is the chance of this pattern?” Students guess. Highlight intuitive vs. formal.

5–15 min VOCAB & MINI-NOTE  
 Direct instruction with questioning:  
  • Experiment vs. outcome vs. sample space (S)  
  • Event (E) as subset of S  
  • Probability formula P(E)=|E|/|S| when outcomes equally likely  
 Class builds sample space for coin (2 outcomes) and die (6 outcomes).

15–30 min GUIDED PRACTICE (Stations or Think-Pair-Share)  
Station A Single coin: P(H), P(T)  
Station B Single die: P(roll >4), P(odd), P(prime)  
Station C Marble bag diagram: 3 red, 2 blue, 1 green. Students list S and compute P(green), P(not red)  
Teacher circulates, checks for misconception (denominator consistency).

30–40 min INTRO TO EXPERIMENTAL PROBABILITY  
 Each pair tosses a coin 20 times, records heads count. Class aggregates data on board. Compare class experimental proportion to 0.5. Discuss Law of Large Numbers qualitatively.

40–47 min COMPOUND INDEPENDENT EVENTS  
 Example: P(rolling a 4 then a 5) with two dice; emphasize independence, multiplication rule P(A and B)=P(A)×P(B) when events independent. Quick practice problems on mini-whiteboards.

47–50 min EXIT TICKET (Formative Assessment)  
 1. Define event.  
 2. Bag has 5 yellow, 3 blue, 2 red. Find P(blue).  
 3. Find P(rolling 6 and then flipping tails).  
Collect, gauge mastery for next period.

Period 2 (Optional Extension / Lab)

0–10 min RECAP & ERROR ANALYSIS  
 Review common exit-ticket errors; students correct.

10–35 min SIMULATION LAB – “Race to 100”  
 Groups choose a random device (dice app or physical). Task: simulate 100 trials of “roll two dice, sum is 7?” Record successes, compute empirical probability, graph running proportion. Compare to theoretical 6/36 = 1/6. Students create line graph of convergence.

35–45 min DISCUSSION & HIGHER-LEVEL QUESTIONING  
 • Why are outcomes on two dice not equally likely for sums?  
 • Introduce sample-space diagram (6×6 matrix) to show nine ways to make 10 vs. six for 7.  
 • Extension challenge: calculate P(sum prime).

45–50 min REFLECTION & REAL-WORLD LINK  
 Exit slip: Write two sentences on how probability can inform real-life decisions (insurance, sports analytics, genetics).

————————————————————————
5. Differentiation & Supports
————————————————————————
Struggling Learners  
 • Provide color-coded sample-space charts  
 • Use smaller numbers (coin only) before dice  
 • Sentence frames for explanations  
Advanced Learners  
 • Conditional probability extension (“If first toss heads, what is P(second toss heads?)”)  
 • Introduce complementary events P(A′)=1−P(A) proofs  
ELL  
 • Visual vocabulary cards (event, outcome) with icons  
 • Pair with bilingual peer for station work  
IEP/504  
 • Extra processing time on stations  
 • Allow calculator for fraction-to-percent conversions  

————————————————————————
6. Assessment
————————————————————————
Formative Exit tickets, whiteboard responses, teacher observation check-list  
Summative Homework set (15 mixed problems) + short quiz next class (10 min) covering vocabulary, single- and two-stage probabilities, and interpreting experimental data

————————————————————————
7. Homework (sample)
————————————————————————
1. A spinner is divided into 8 equal sectors (3 red, 2 blue, 2 green, 1 yellow). Find the probability of:  
 a) landing on red b) not green c) blue or yellow  
2. Two independent coin flips. Write sample space, compute P(exactly one head).  
3. Deck of 52 cards. Find P(drawing a heart).  
4. Challenge: What is the probability of rolling doubles with two fair dice? Show reasoning.

————————————————————————
8. Teacher Reflection (post-lesson)
————————————————————————
Note timing of stations; examine aggregated experimental vs. theoretical discrepancies. Adjust future lessons to address independence misconceptions.

————————————————————————
End of Lesson Plan
